newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian consumers opening wallets, survey says.
newsitem.headline: Canadian consumers opening wallets, survey says.

text.p: An improving job market has convinced a majority of Canadians to loosen the purse strings and make a major purchase, said a survey released on Thursday by a Canadian economic institute.
The Conference Board of Canada said that 59.4 percent of consumers polled in the Summer 1997 Index of Consumer Attitudes felt that this summer was a good time to buy so-called "big ticket items."

The board said the surge in consumer confidence was reflected in the index of consumer attitudes, which had reached a seven-year high of 116.2. At the same time, the index of business confidence continued to set record highs, rising 4.9 points to set a new record of 165, the board added.
Both surveys were conducted in early June 1997.

"The improving job picture has clearly hit home," said Paul Darby, director of the board's economic services. "Given the recent employment surge, the number of people expecting further improvement in the coming six months reached a 10-quarter high of 21.6 percent."
Flat interest rates, which are at a 40-year low of 4.75 percent, have given Canadian consumers an extra comfort zone, the board said.

"Low interest rates have helped maintain the proportion of consumers who now is a good time to buy big-ticket items," Darby said. "Accordingly, real consumer spending on durable goods has increased in excess of eight percent since mid-1996."
The board also noted rising business optimism as the number of firms planning to undertake capital expenditures edged up 1.3 percent from the first quarter to 77.4 percent.
